authorization_and_limitations.hash_limit: Hashes bind exact bytes; they do not prove real daemon cleanup, runtime identities, remote absence, kernel behavior or experiment occurrence.
not_performed: Docker calls or mutations, including Docker help/version
source, worktree, frozen snapshot or earlier artifact edits
authorization_and_limitations.performed_only: Static reads, pinned hashing, offline unit tests, dictionary-backed fake Docker calls, and bounded benign local Python pipe/supervisor fixtures. All review script invocations used Python -B; test runs used ResourceWarning-as-error. TMPDIR and persistent review output were confined to correctness.

findings.description: DockerBackend.wait constructs container wait --condition not-running ID. The condition parameter is an Engine API wait option, not a docker container wait CLI flag. The installed read-only bash and zsh completion references expose no such wait flag. This branch is reached for every present owned container, including already stopped/created ones.
findings.expected: Present owned stopped containers can be waited for and removed with supported closed CLI arguments, then unattached owned volumes can be removed.
findings.impact: The watchdog's ordinary cleanup route is nonfunctional for any present container. It correctly refuses completion rather than falsely certifying absence, but leaves owned resources unresolved even in the no-fault path.
findings.limitation: No Docker executable, help command, daemon request, or real cleanup was run. CLI compatibility was assessed statically and exercised by a contract-faithful fake runner.
findings.recommendation: Consider using [container, wait, exact_id], whose default wait condition is not-running, and retaining the subsequent independent stopped/Pid=0 inspection. Add a fake CLI argument-contract test for the full DockerBackend cleanup path, rather than testing cleanup only against FakeDocker.wait.
reproduction: Run independent_probes.IndependentProbes.test_cleanup_uses_supported_wait_cli_grammar with the supplied fake runner only.
Prepare three synthetic owned containers and two synthetic volumes, then call owned_resources.cleanup through the real DockerBackend with MetadataCLI as runner.
The CLI grammar model rejects --condition for each wait. Cleanup catches the resulting DOCKER_FAILED before remove; all three container objects and both attached volume objects remain.
findings.title: Unsupported Docker wait flag prevents owned container and dependent volume disposal

findings.description: _send rejects queued complete frames and EOF but ignores decoder.partial. A response already observed before its enabling input becomes acceptable if only its final newline arrives after that input.
findings.expected: Output bytes already buffered for a response that requires G or R cannot be legitimized by completing the frame after the enabling send.
findings.impact: The adapter can report a valid final native phase even though the response began before start/resume dispatch. Canonical JSON and bounded framing alone do not establish protocol causality.
findings.limitation: Only benign Python helpers were executed. The finding is stream-order acceptance, not a claim that the primitive certified remote absence or that a native/kernel run occurred.
findings.recommendation: Consider treating any pending decoder.partial bytes, as well as complete frames and EOF, as early actor output before case/start/resume writes. Retain the existing close/reap failure path and add atomic READY-plus-partial-FINISHED and HELD-plus-partial-CONTINUATION regressions.
reproduction: A benign Python target reads its case, atomically writes READY plus FINISHED without the final LF, and then waits for G.

receive(READY) leaves all 32 bytes of the FINISHED JSON in decoder.partial. start_target nevertheless sends G. The helper then writes LF, receive(FINISHED) accepts it, and finish_transport returns normally.
The observer counterpart writes ARMED, HELD, and the 47-byte CONTINUATION_DISPATCHED JSON without LF before waiting for R; it is also accepted after the delayed LF.
A complete early FINISHED frame is rejected by the control probe, isolating the defect to fragmented output at the input boundary.
findings.title: Buffered partial responses bypass send-before-read phase ordering

findings.description: verify_attachments checks the exact attachment allowlist during preparation. open_actor revalidates both volume identities and the actor's mounts, but performs no attachment query. A foreign container attaching after prepare_resources leaves all those other checks unchanged and reaches the start factory.
findings.expected: A start-admission API either rechecks exact allowed volume attachments or has an explicit, enforceable caller precondition for that check.
findings.impact: Volume identity and own mount correctness do not establish exclusive owned access. A future caller relying on the apparent final metadata revalidation in open_actor could activate a target with a foreign control/witness attacher.
findings.limitation: This is a start-API contract gap, not a demand that the acknowledged pending runtime dispatcher or kernel admission already be implemented. No real actor start occurred.
findings.recommendation: Consider passing the acknowledged registry inventory or its exact attachment allowlists into open_actor and invoking the existing attachment verifier immediately before dispatch. If this is intentionally delegated to the pending dispatcher, document and enforce that activation precondition rather than leaving it implicit.
reproduction: Prepare a valid synthetic registry, then add a foreign full container ID to FakeDocker.foreign_attachments for the control volume.
Call the real DockerBackend.open_actor with MetadataCLI and a stream factory that only records argv and starts no process.
The fake stream factory is reached once, with zero attachment-list queries; the foreign attachment is not refused.
findings.title: Make attachment revalidation an explicit part of the actor-start contract

findings.description: close sets closed=True and sends a cleanup request before attempting to read the final reply. If the independent lifetime trigger has already produced and queued cleanup and the worker has exited, the send raises BrokenPipeError. The finally block closes the channel, discarding the unread result and preventing subsequent wait_for_cleanup through the public API.
findings.expected: Cleanup collection tolerates the independent trigger winning the race with an explicit close request and validates the final reply before retiring the channel.
findings.impact: This loses parent-side result reconciliation on an ordinary expiry race. The worker did perform its simulated cleanup and retained its journal; this finding is not a claim of child cleanup failure or false absence.
findings.recommendation: Consider a unified final-result collection path that drains an already available reply and handles a broken request write by still attempting the bounded receive/validation. Preserve finally-based channel closure and arrange worker joining even when request transmission or result validation fails.
reproduction: Start WatchdogProcess with absent_backend, a private temporary journal directory, and lifetime_seconds=0.7; publish generation zero.
Join the benign worker with a two-second test bound after its independent deadline. Confirm its retained journal ends with a valid deadline cleanup.
Call close. It raises BrokenPipeError despite the final cleanup reply already being available; the object becomes closed.
findings.title: close loses an already queued final watchdog result when the worker has exited

independent_tests.fake_evidence_caveat: The subject DockerBackend labels its return objects docker_metadata_only even when supplied a fake runner. All Docker metadata and start commands in this review were simulated; none are real daemon evidence.
independent_tests.harness_history: The initial 15-probe attempt had one review-harness error: the write-confinement audit hook rejected Popen opening /dev/null O_RDWR for stdin. Only the review harness was adjusted to allow that nonpersistent device. The original logs are retained. Both final 17-probe runs have zero errors, the same five assertion failures, and byte-identical observation logs.
independent_tests.probe_failure_interpretation: Five expected-correct assertions fail and reproduce four issues; two assertions cover the same fragmented-phase defect. Final runs have no unexpected errors or skips.

inputs.base_commit_binding: User-supplied base, consistent with the preserved foundation manifest; review is bound to every intake snapshot byte.

positive_observations: Registry publishes each candidate before create and each identity before preparation can progress; supplied ambiguous-create tests exercise all five roles without retry.
All eleven independent resource-prefix vectors retain incomplete cleanup whenever any candidate is unbound, including when every candidate name is absent.

Foreign ownership and foreign attachments leave the affected resources unresolved while independent safe cleanup continues. Closed-selector probes reject short/uppercase IDs, slash aliases, options, unowned volume names and image tags before runner invocation.

Observer-only exact target PID namespace membership and the oracle's private PID namespace are represented consistently. Observer mounts remain empty. No new runtime capability is inferred from those metadata predicates.

Strict canonical JSON framing passes 496 independent three-fragment partitions. Complete early frames, duplicate/truncated private-control frames, stderr, output bounds and deadlines are refused in the supplied/independent checks.

Command stdout/stderr are drained with bounded capture. A departed benign local leader with a child holding its pipes causes group kill before leader reaping; no process-group or remote-container absence is inferred from normal EOF.

A real benign separate-session watchdog acknowledges all eleven generations, retains fourteen journal rows, and stays within 23299 control bytes for the fixture. Journal replacement is rejected using file identity. Supplied tests also exercise actual benign owner-process exit.

The watchdog default authorizer predicate permits only cleanup for the exact scope hash; create, start and actor input remain unauthorized. This was checked without executing the default Docker runner.

preservation.measurement_scope: The full frozen snapshot and five root prior artifacts were hashed before any tests and after all tests. Supplemental checks compared 61 implementation-worktree overlay paths, eight native build inputs, eleven original retained build artifacts, fourteen frozen foundation exports and two installed static CLI references against their pinned values before the final probe runs and after all tests. The concurrently used main worktree was not claimed to be globally unchanged; no review write targeted any worktree.

recommendation: Remediate COR-ADAPTER-001 and COR-ADAPTER-002 in a separately authorized implementation worktree, clarify/tighten the two P2 contracts, and refreeze for an independent rerun of the targeted regressions plus the existing suite. No runtime/native experiment is requested or authorized by this review.

excluded_and_acknowledged_pending: trial dispatcher and full receipt assembly
included: safe per-resource cleanup and creation settlement
bounded canonical actor streams and local process handling
separate-session host watchdog, private byte IPC, retained journal and final-result reconciliation

summary: The foundation boundaries and several new fail-closed invariants are sound, and all 71 supplied tests pass independently. Two reproducible adapter blockers remain: unsupported cleanup wait argv and fragmented early-response acceptance. Two additional start/result-collection contract issues should be addressed. This review does not reopen the prior foundation GO or authorize any runtime experiment.
